narrative: The model estimated a 65.1% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt, meaning failure was judged more likely than passing; that prediction is why your law school application was rejected. This is a probability, not a certainty, but it crossed the denial threshold. The strongest factor was your third-year class rank: you were in the second decile, well below the 5.79 average among admitted students, and this pushed the prediction most strongly toward failure. Your first-year rank, third decile versus an admitted average of sixth decile, was the second most influential factor and also increased the predicted risk. Your LSAT score of 30, below the admitted average of 37.18, was the third-ranked factor; in this prediction it acted as a modest pull toward passing, but it could not offset the academic-rank signals. To move forward, ask admissions whether you can submit additional context or appeal, such as an explanation of circumstances affecting your early grades, evidence of later improvement, a concrete bar-preparation plan, and a higher LSAT retake if feasible. Also speak with a prelaw advisor about strengthening your application before reapplying.
